content.title: About
content.content: Steamed whiting is a delicate white fish with low fat content and high-quality protein. Steaming preserves most of its nutrients, making it an excellent choice for healthy eating.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Whiting belongs to the cod family and is widely distributed in northern seas.
Steaming retains the fish’s natural flavor without adding extra fats.
Whiting is a good source of B‑group vitamins, especially B12, which supports the nervous system.
In the wild, whiting can grow over 100 cm, but culinary portions usually use smaller specimens.
Whiting is a traditional ingredient in Scandinavian and Russian cuisines.

items.title: High‑quality protein
items.content: Whiting provides complete protein needed for tissue growth and repair.

items.title: Low in fat
items.content: Steamed whiting contains very little saturated fat, suitable for low‑fat diets.

items.title: Rich in iodine
items.content: Iodine supports thyroid function and hormone production.

items.title: B‑vitamins
items.content: Vitamin B12 and B6 aid metabolism and nervous system health.

items.title: Minerals
items.content: Whiting supplies selenium, phosphorus, and magnesium, important for bones and antioxidant protection.

items.title: Fish allergy
items.content: Some individuals may experience allergic reactions to fish, including whiting.

items.title: Heavy‑metal contamination
items.content: In certain regions fish may contain traces of mercury or other heavy metals; choose reputable sources.

items.title: Sodium content
items.content: If the fish is pre‑salted, consider its contribution to daily sodium intake.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Steamed whiting can be served as a main dish, added to salads, soups, or used in wraps. It pairs well with lemon, fresh herbs (dill, parsley) and light yogurt‑based sauces.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store fresh whiting in the refrigerator at 0‑2 °C in an airtight container for up to 2 days. Frozen fish can be kept at –18 °C for up to 3 months. Before cooking, check for any off‑odors.
